author: Moiwen
quote:
After playing GTA VI, I honestly can't understand how so many critics are giving this game a perfect 99/100. I went into it with high expectations, especially considering Rockstar's reputation, the enormous development budget, and all the years we've waited for this game. Unfortunately, what I got was a huge disappointment.

I'll give credit where it's due. The graphics are impressive, the world looks beautiful, and the level of visual detail is incredible. But graphics alone don't make a great game, and they certainly shouldn't be enough to justify a perfect score.

My biggest problem is the lack of freedom.

GTA has always been about exploring a massive open world, experimenting, causing chaos, and doing things your own way. Yet in GTA VI, I constantly feel like the game is telling me what I can and cannot do.

For example, there are certain NPCs, including activist characters, that I can't attack or shoot. I'm not saying attacking those characters should be the purpose of the game. My point is that when a sandbox game starts placing arbitrary restrictions on which fictional characters you can interact with, it breaks the illusion of freedom.

The relationship system is another major disappointment.

From what I've experienced, the only intimate relationship option outside of Lucia involves a male ex-partner. Why are the choices so limited? Why can't I pursue other relationships, be unfaithful, or interact with adult characters in different ways?

I'm not against the existence of same-sex relationships in video games. What bothers me is feeling that certain creative or ideological decisions are being prioritized over player freedom. I don't want Rockstar deciding which relationships I should explore. I want meaningful choices and the freedom to make them myself.

For a game that constantly emphasizes realism and freedom, the actual possibilities feel surprisingly restricted.

Then there are the physics.

The game looks realistic in screenshots and trailers, but the illusion often falls apart when you actually interact with the world. Some physical interactions simply don't feel convincing. It's frustrating to see so much attention given to visual details while other fundamental aspects of gameplay feel underdeveloped.

I've also encountered plenty of bugs, which makes those perfect review scores even harder to understand. How can a game with noticeable technical problems receive a flawless rating?

Performance is another issue. We're in 2026, and GTA VI is still limited to 30 FPS on PS5 Pro. I understand that a massive open world requires considerable processing power, but that doesn't mean performance should suddenly stop being part of the evaluation.

Other games have been criticized for failing to reach 60 FPS, suffering frame drops, or having optimization problems. Why should GTA VI be treated differently?

And then there's the story.

Despite the enormous budget and technological advances, we're still dealing with a largely linear narrative. I expected more meaningful decisions, different outcomes, and greater control over how the story develops.

A beautiful open world doesn't automatically mean a game offers genuine freedom. You can explore an enormous map and still feel restricted by its systems.

What disappoints me most is that Rockstar had the resources, time, and experience to push the genre much further. Instead, I feel like too much attention went into presentation while some of the things that actually matter to me as a player were neglected.

And this brings me to professional reviews.

I'm tired of seeing inconsistent standards in gaming journalism. Some games lose points for technical limitations, bugs, restrictive mechanics, or a lack of innovation, while others seem almost immune to criticism because of their name and reputation.

If a reviewer gives GTA VI a perfect 100/100 while acknowledging significant shortcomings, I think they owe readers a convincing explanation of why those shortcomings don't affect the final score.

I'm not claiming every positive review is dishonest, and I'm not saying people shouldn't enjoy this game. But I do believe that professional critics should be consistent, transparent, and willing to judge every game by comparable standards.

A massive budget doesn't guarantee quality. A famous developer doesn't guarantee innovation. And impressive graphics don't automatically make a game a masterpiece.I wanted GTA VI to be extraordinary. 

I wanted a world that felt genuinely alive, with believable physics, meaningful interactions, freedom to experiment, and a level of technical polish worthy of its reputation.

Instead, I got a visually stunning game that feels far more limited than I expected.

For me, GTA VI is a massive disappointment. Not because it has nothing good to offer, but because it had the potential to be so much more.

And that's exactly why I can't agree with those perfect scores.

author: Moiwen
quote:
I've been really impressed with Ocarina of Time Remake. And honestly, it's not just because of the graphics or the nostalgia. What surprised me the most is how different the game actually feels compared to the original.

The first thing I noticed was how incredibly smooth Link feels to control. He's light, fast, and responsive, and every action feels almost instant. Moving around, attacking, dodging, and interacting with the world all feel so natural. There's no annoying delay between pressing a button and seeing Link react. The controls just feel right.

The performance makes everything even better. Having a consistent 60 FPS without noticeable drops throughout my playthrough makes a huge difference, especially during combat and exploration. Everything feels fluid, and I never had that frustrating feeling of fighting against the controls.

Another thing I absolutely loved was the sound design. The soundtrack is fantastic, but what really caught my attention was how the music dynamically changes depending on what you're doing. Even something as simple as standing still or moving around can change how the music plays. It's one of those little details that you might not notice immediately, but once you do, you really appreciate the work behind it. The sound effects, atmosphere, and music all come together beautifully.

Hyrule itself looks incredible. The entire world has been reworked, and the art direction is outstanding. Every area feels more detailed, more alive, and more carefully designed, while still keeping the atmosphere and identity of the original. It's familiar, but at the same time, exploring it feels fresh again.

And that's probably what I appreciate the most about this remake. They didn't just improve the graphics and call it a day.

The gameplay mechanics have been redesigned, boss fights feel much better, and the new shortcuts for weapons and equipment make a massive difference. Switching between items is faster and more convenient, and you spend far less time navigating menus. These improvements might sound small individually, but together they completely change how the game feels.

I also really appreciate how well they preserved the original story. Despite all the changes, it still feels like Ocarina of Time at its core. The addition of voice acting in multiple languages is another welcome improvement that makes the experience feel more modern.

That said, there is one area where I wish they had gone a little further: Hyrule's lore.

There are so many mysteries in this world that could've been explored in more detail. I would've loved to learn more about Ganondorf's past, his upbringing, and what led him down the path he eventually took. He's such an important character, and I feel like there's still so much of his story that could be told.

The Bottom of the Well in Kakariko Village is another example. That place has always had a dark and mysterious atmosphere, especially with its connections to the Sheikah. I would've loved to discover more about what happened there and what the Sheikah were actually doing.

And then there's the Temple of Light. We receive the Light Medallion, but we never get to explore a proper dungeon dedicated to it. I really wish they had taken the opportunity to finally give us a Temple of Light, with its own puzzles, secrets, and maybe even a new boss.

A few additional areas, more meaningful side quests, and some extra stories about Hyrule would've made the experience even better. I'm not talking about adding content just to make the game longer. I mean content that actually expands the world, answers some of its mysteries, and gives us something genuinely new to discover.

I wouldn't have wanted them to change the original story. I think preserving it was absolutely the right decision. But expanding on the things we never got to learn would've been amazing.

That's really the only reason I can't call it a perfect 10.

For me, this remake is proof that you can respect a classic while completely modernizing the experience. The controls, performance, music, art direction, redesigned mechanics, and improved boss fights make it feel like a genuinely new game rather than just an old one with prettier graphics.

I enjoyed every moment of it, and I think the developers did an incredible job. I just wish they'd been a little more ambitious when it came to expanding Hyrule's history and giving us some new adventures within that world.

My personal score: 9.6/10.

Unfortunately, Metacritic doesn't allow decimal scores, so I'll be giving it a 10. I don't think rounding my 9.6 down to a 9 would be fair to the game, especially when it would unnecessarily bring down its overall rating. A 10 is simply a closer reflection of how highly I rate this remake.

An amazing remake, and one of the best gaming experiences I've had in a long time.
game_title: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time
